description:
I am a solo web developer (React / Next.js / Frontend logic) participating in this year's hackathon as a one-man army. My goal for the weekend is to build a highly interactive, fast, and clean web application using modern workflows like VS Code and Claude Code.

I specialize in API integrations, state management, and turning raw data into engaging UI/UX. I enjoy blending hard technical constraints with a bit of absurd humor and creative interfaces, completely avoiding heavy hardware :0
summary:
P.U.R.R. Command Center (Planetary Utility for Regolith Reconnaissance) is a web app that scores every patch of land on Earth for how well it could stand in for four planned base sites: Shackleton crater rim and a lava-tube pit in Mare Tranquillitatis on the Moon, and Jezero crater and Arcadia Planitia on Mars.

Known analog sites are mostly hand-picked, so I wanted a systematic search instead. A Python pipeline combines seven global datasets (NASA MODIS, MERRA-2, NOAA ETOPO and a lithology map) into 341,212 land cells and scores each one against each target. The scoring rules were frozen in git before I ran any validation, and known NASA analogs end up in the top percentiles while look-alike "traps" like the Amazon don't.

The app turns this into something you can actually use: plan a base, then swipe through Earth analogs like Tinder, guided by Félicette, the real cat that flew to space in 1963. Every card shows where the analogy holds, where it breaks, and what you could test there. Funny detail: Félicette's own launch pad in the Sahara turned out to be a strong Jezero analog.
details:
What it does

P.U.R.R. Command Center helps answer a simple question: where on Earth should we rehearse a Moon or Mars base? You pick a target (Shackleton rim, the Mare Tranquillitatis lava-tube pit, Jezero or Arcadia Planitia) and describe your mission: how big the base is, what rovers you bring, and whether it's robotic, a short crewed stay or a permanent base. Then you get a deck of Earth sites to swipe. PURR to accept, HISS to reject.

Each card has real satellite imagery (NASA GIBS, and ESA Sentinel-2 for single sites) that you can switch to NDVI or surface temperature, plus two separate scores. The Analog Score is planetary similarity from a frozen method. Mission Fit is about your mission (slopes, area, local resources like ice or basalt) and it never changes the Analog Score. A radar chart shows every dimension and highlights the one that holds the site back. After each swipe you get a breakdown: where the analogy holds, where it breaks, what global data can't see (mineralogy, caves, buried ice), what you could test there, and a comparison with real Moon and Mars values from LRO Diviner, LOLA, Mars 2020 MEDA and MRO SHARAD studies, with DOIs.

There's also a map where you can click any point on Earth and see how it scores for all four targets, with a plain-language reason when the score is low. Kraków for example gets 4/100 because it's too green and too wet. A report tab collects your picks, the validation results and Earth's limits (gravity, vacuum, radiation).

How it works

All the heavy work runs once, offline, in a Python pipeline. It downloads seven global datasets for 2023 (NASA MODIS NDVI, land surface temperature and land cover, NASA MERRA-2 precipitation and dust, NOAA ETOPO 2022 relief and the GLiM lithology map), puts them on one 0.25 degree grid and scores every land cell. Each dimension gets a 0-1 score for how far Earth gets toward the planetary condition. Measuring distance to Mars directly doesn't work, because no place on Earth is anywhere near -236 C or 6 mbar. The dimensions are combined with a weighted geometric mean, so a single failing dimension (a forest, for example) sinks the site.

To keep myself honest I committed the scoring config to git before running any validation, and logged every later change in a method log. Results: known NASA analog sites land at median percentiles of 75-99.6 depending on the target, traps at 11-21, and that holds across 200 Monte Carlo runs with jittered weights and thresholds. The method also surfaced less-known candidates like the Haruj and Harrat lava fields (lunar lava tubes), Dasht-e Lut and the Taklamakan (Jezero), and Canadian Arctic islands (Arcadia). I also document where it's weak, like the thin margin for the lava-tube target.

The web app is a static Next.js site on Vercel. It reads the pipeline output and calls NASA GIBS, NASA POWER and Sentinel-2 tiles live, so there's no backend.

Why it matters / who it's for

Mission and rover teams can shortlist field-test sites that fit a concrete mission. Analog researchers get a transparent, reproducible global method with sources on every card. Students and the public learn why "looks like Mars" isn't the same as "is like Mars", which is the whole point of the trap cards.

Tools

Python (earthaccess, xarray, numpy, rasterio, geopandas), Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, Framer Motion, Recharts, Vitest, Playwright, Vercel. EN/PL interface, mobile-first.

Code: https://github.com/ner4m1x/nasa-felicette-2026

Limits: Earth can't reproduce lunar or martian gravity, vacuum or radiation, the grid is about 28 km and covers one year of data, and global data can't see minerals or caves. All of this is stated in the app.
